Copper hollow fiber electrode for efficient CO2 electroreduction
Chang Zhu a,b,1, Guofei Shen a,1, Wei Chen a,b,*, Xiao Dong a, Guihua Li a, Yanfang Song a, Wei Wei a,b,c,**, Yuhan Sun a,c,d,***
a CAS Key Laboratory of Low-Carbon Conversion Science and Engineering, Shanghai Advanced Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, 201210, PR China b University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100049, PR China c School of Physical Science and Technology, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, 201210, PR China d Shanghai Institute of Clean Technology, Shanghai, 201620, PR China
H I G H L I G H T S G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
• Copper hollow fiber is constructed by a phase-inversion/sintering process. • CO2 effective activation and compulsive interaction lead to efficient conversion. • HCOOH yield reaches 2677 μmol∙h− 1∙cm− 2 with as high as current density 210 mA∙cm− 2.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: CO2 electroreduction Formate Cu hollow fiber Gas-diffusion electrode
A B S T R A C T
Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to useful chemicals is a prospective strategy that can address both carbon emission abatement and sustainable energy development. Due to the low solubility and intrinsic inertness of CO2, efficient CO2 conversion remains a challenge in aqueous CO2 electroreduction. Herein we report that a copper hollow fiber of gas-diffusion electrode constructed by a phase-inversion/sintering process enables CO2 reduction to formate maintains considerable faradaic efficiency (80%) at high current density (210 mA∙cm− 2), delivering its formate yield about 16 and 30 times those of copper foam and copper foil, respectively. CO2 molecules are forced to penetrate through the porous wall of Cu hollow fiber electrode, resulting in CO2 effective activation and compulsive interaction with active sites, which synergistically facilitates formate formation. This work indicates a positive potentiality of employ a distinct gas-diffusion electrode of hollow fiber to optimize reaction kinetics for efficient and selective electroreduction of CO2 to formate.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The worldwide increase in CO2 emissions has triggered related energy crisis and environmental issues [1–3]. Driven by renewable electricity from wind, solar, etc [4,5], the CO2 electroreduction reaction (CO2ERR) can abate CO2 emission, meanwhile convert intermittent renewable electricity into high-energy-density compounds, exhibiting promising application potential. Although CO2ERR as a hot topic has been widely studied for over few decades, high-efficiency CO2 conversion remains challenging due to slow and divergent kinetics of CO2 reduction, which is derived from the poor solubility of CO2 in electrolyte solution and intrinsic inertness of CO2, at the same time with competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [6–8].
In order to alleviate low CO2 solubility and suppress HER, the tactic of fabricating gas-diffusion electrode was frequently adopted, which resulted in significant promotions for electroreducing CO2 [9–16]. Diaz-Sainz et al. reported that formate with ~90% faradaic efficiency (FE) in CO2ERR was achieved over the gas-diffusion electrode comprising hydrophobic binder (polytetrafluoroethylene, PTFE), conductive addition, and bismuth nanoparticles [14]. Yang et al. demonstrated the production of formate at current densities up to 200 mA∙cm− 2 and FE ranging between 73 and 91% using the gas diffusion electrode [15]. Klemm et al. integrated as-prepared tin oxide into the gas diffusion electrodes and obtained an average FE of formate at least 80% with the current density of 1000 mA∙cm− 2 [16]. However, the multiple components and subtle configurations of the traditional gas-diffusion electrodes requires complicated fabrication procedures, which may hinder their large-scale applications [17–20]. In addition, the integrated binders may age and loose in the long-term electrolysis, encumbering the performance stability of CO2 reduction [21]. Considering these problems encountered in fabrication and application of the traditional gas-diffusion electrodes, it is necessary to use a tougher gas-diffusion electrode fabricated by a simple method.
Here, we adopt commercial copper powder to fabricate porous copper hollow fiber (Cu HF) through a phase inversion/sintering composite process (see Supplementary Information (SI) and Fig. S1 for details), which is only composed of metallic copper (Fig. S2) with hierarchical pore structures. The sintered Cu particles constructing Cu HF not only build a tough self-supported gas-diffusion electrode without any binder, but also induce the synergetic promotion for CO2ERR while the competitive hydrogen evolution was also suppressed. Cu HF possesses a considerable electroreducing CO2-to-formate capability comparable to the excellent catalyst electrodes reported in Table S1. This may exhibit a promising potential to promote the CO2 electroreduction efficiency by using a hollow fiber gas-diffusion electrode.

sections.heading: 2.1. Cu hollow fiber electrode fabrication
sections.text:
Cu hollow fiber electrode was fabricated by a traditional phaseinversion/sintering process. Briefly, commercially available Cu powder (purity 99%, average size of 500 nm) was used as an inorganic phase in the electrode preparation, N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP, 99.5%) and Polyetherimide (PEI, Ultem 1000) were used as solvent and polymer, respectively (Fig. S1). Cu powder (60 wt%), NMP (30 wt%) and PEI (10 wt%) were ball-milled and uniformly mixed to form casting solution, and then the bubbles were removed in a vacuum overnight. The casting solution was extruded through the spinning machine and solidified in the tap water bath. Directly after spinning the as-formed tubes were kept in a water bath for 24 h for completion of the solvent elimination, followed by drying and stretching for 48 h to obtain the green body.
The green bodies were firstly sintered in air at 600 ◦C for 4 h to remove PEI. After being naturally cooled to room temperature, the oxidized green bodies were then reduced in 5% H2 (Argon balance) at 500 ◦C for 3 h to obtain metallic Cu of hollow fiber. The as-obtained Cu
hollow fibers were stored in Argon atmosphere. The Cu HF with an exposed length of 3 cm was stuck into a copper tube using conductive silver adhesive for electrical contact (see SI for details). And the end of Cu HF and the joint as well as the partial copper tube was sealed and coated with epoxy (Fig. S6A). After drying for 12 h, the Cu HF electrode was obtained.

sections.heading: 2.2. Materials characterization
sections.text: Hollow fiber morphology test was carried out with Zeiss SUPRA 55 SAPPHIRE scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and the acceleration voltage was 3.0 kV. XRD tested by using a Rigaku Ultima 4 X-ray diffractometer with a Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) at 40 kV and 40 mA, and the scanning speed was 2◦∙min− 1. A Titan ST microscope was used to obtain a TEM image at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The XPS spectrum was obtained by running with Thermo K-ALPHA XPS instrument with a monochromatic Al Kα source (1486.6 eV) Quantum 2000 scanning ESCA microprobe. The peaks of Cu XPS and Cu auger were recorded in the binding energy ranges of 925–965 eV and 555–585 eV, respectively. The gas permeability of Cu hollow fiber was determined by virtue of measuring and analyzing the behaviors of CH4, N2, H2 and CO2 under different transmembrane pressure drops.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical measurement
sections.text:
The electrochemical experiment of CO2ERR was conducted in two chamber reactors with a three-electrode system at room temperature (Figs. S6B and C). The electrolyte was 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, and CO2 gas was introduced for about 30 min before the experiment to saturate the CO2 in the solution (Fig. S6D). The potential range of LSV was 0.0 ~ − 1.4 V vs. RHE and the scan rate was 10 mV∙s− 1. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were performed at a potential of − 0.9 V and the frequency range was from 100 kHz to 1 Hz. The cyclic voltammetry curve was obtained by performing different scan speeds, the electric double-layer capacitance of the electrode can be obtained from the dependence of the non-Faradaic capacitance current on the scanning rate and used to evaluate the electrochemical active area (ECSA). The potentials involved in the experiment were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) using E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/ AgCl) + 0.197 V + 0.0591 × pH.
The reaction exhaust was directly passed into a gas chromatograph (GC-2014, Shimadzu) equipped with a molecular sieve-13 × 60/80 column and a Plot-Q80/100 column for online detection and analysis. According to the peak area, the amount of H2 and CO in the product can be calculated. Formate was detected and analyzed with a 600 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker) and DSS and D2O were internal standards.

sections.heading: 3.1. Characterizations of Cu hollow fiber
sections.text:
Fig. 1A shows the as-fabricated Cu HF with a metallic luster, similar to Cu foil. Typical SEM images (Fig. 1B and Fig. S3) of the outer and inner surfaces of Cu HF exhibit the abundant pores evenly distributed, possessing a pore size range of 200–300 nm (the inset in Fig. 1B). No initial spherical Cu particles (Fig. S4) are discerned from the smooth surface of Cu HF, implying the well-fused substrate constructed by sintering. The wall thickness of Cu HF is ~200 μm and the cross-sectional morphology exhibits characteristic fingerlike porous structures in the outer/inner regions without microvoids formed (Fig. 1C and D).
The permeances of H2, CH4, N2 and CO2 through Cu HF remain almost constant at different pressure drops (Fig. 2A), and the gas permeances are inversely proportional to the square roots of their molecular weights (Fig. 2B), implying Knudsen gas diffusion transported through Cu HF [22–24]. In addition, the average pore size determined by gas permeation is 270 nm (see SI for details), in agreement with SEM
C. Zhu et al.
Journal of Power Sources 495 (2021) 229814
observations. The XRD pattern of Cu HF is indexed to metallic Cu (111), (200) and (220) planes (JCPDS no. 04–0836), the same as that of the commercial self-supported Cu foam (Fig. 3A). In contrast, Cu foil exhibits the weakest (111) peak while the most intense (220) peak, indicating the predominantly exposed (220) facet. The HRTEM further revealed the surfaces of Cu HF are metallic copper substrates, and the d-spacing is 2.08 Å, which corresponds to the lattice fringes of Cu (111) (Fig. S3), consistent with the XRD results. Moreover, both XPS and Auger spectra show that the outer/inner surfaces of Cu HF consist of only metallic Cu0 species, which are also highly similar to Cu foam and Cu foil (Fig. 3B). This result shows that the bulk and surface compositions of Cu HF are completely identical to those of Cu foam, and Cu foil possesses the metallic Cu0 surface while preferred (220) plane.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical measurements and CO2ERR performance
sections.text:
The electrochemical behaviors of the electrodes were shown by the linear sweep of the voltammetry curve (Fig. 4A). The LSV curves of Cu HF show that the onset potentials in both Ar and CO2 were − 0.4 V, and relatively larger current densities remained in CO2 in the whole range of − 0.4 to − 1.4 V (the inset in Fig. 4A), implying the occurrence of CO2ERR and HER. While the onset potentials of Cu foil and Cu foam delayed to − 0.7 V, and their current densities were only about 11% and 15% of that of Cu HF at − 1.4 V, indicating their low electrocatalytic activities due to the less active sites on Cu foil and Cu foam. The electrochemical active areas (ECSAs) of Cu foil and Cu foam are 1.4 and 0.8 mF∙cm− 2, respectively, much lower than that of Cu HF (4.7 mF∙cm− 2) (vide infra). Moreover, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results presented using Nyquist plots (Fig. S5) were fitted to obtain the corresponding equivalent circuit component values (see SI for details). Cu HF had a smaller charge transfer resistance (Rct) compared to Cu foam and Cu foil, indicating favorable reduction kinetics occurred on Cu HF, in agreement with the previous reports [25–27].
The potentiostatic CO2 reduction was performed with free-standing Cu HF, Cu foam and Cu foil as the working electrodes in the cathodic compartment, respectively (Fig. S6), and product detection and analysis were performed by online gas chromatography (GC) and proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H NMR) (Fig. S7). Fig. 4B shows that CO2ERR on Cu HF, Cu foam and Cu foil repeatedly generate CO and formate with a considerable amount of H2 that comes from HER. The reactions on Cu foil and Cu foam were primarily by hydrogen evolution reaction (55–70% FE) with formate and CO as subordinate products in the potential range of − 0.8 to − 1.0 V. In contrast, Cu HF greatly inhibited the occurrence of HER, and the H2 FE decreased to 14% at − 0.9 V. Moreover, the formation of CO was significantly suppressed and the CO FEs at all potentials were below 1% on Cu HF. Thus, formate was predominantly produced on Cu HF.
Fig. 4C shows formate yields of Cu foil, Cu foam and Cu HF electrodes under different potentials. Both Cu foil and Cu foam delivered slowly increasing formate yields from − 0.4 to − 1.1 V, and their formate yields were 88 and 167 μmol h− 1 cm− 2 at − 1.1 V, respectively. In sharp contrast, formate yields of Cu HF present quick increases: linear increase from − 0.4 to − 0.6 V, then exponential increase from − 0.7 to − 0.9 V, followed by a slight slowdown after − 1.0 V. At − 1.1 V, the formate yield of Cu HF reached as high as 2677 μmol h− 1 cm− 2, about 16 and 30 times those of Cu foam and Cu foil, respectively. Actually, such high formate yields and their potential-dependent variation of Cu HF exhibit comparable to the reported electrocatalysts (Table S1) [28]. Note that the hollow fiber copper electrode reported by Kas et al. produced dominant CO rather than formate from electrochemical CO2 reduction on the large three-phase boundaries [29]. This means the pore structures of Cu HF play a crucial role in CO2ERR, which may induce the synergistic effects to alter the route of CO2 reduction (vide infra). Furthermore, the good durability of Cu HF was ensured to have considerably stable electrocatalytic performance with almost constant current density and an inappreciable attenuation in the formate FE after electrochemical reaction at − 0.9 V for 120 h (Fig. S8 and Table S2). The post-reaction XRD and XPS analyses (Figs. S9 and S10) shows that the bulk and surface compositions of Cu HF after the reaction were almost the same as those before the reaction, which is responsible for the stable CO2ERR performances.
The ECSAs were calibrated by the double-layer capacitance obtained by the cyclic voltammetry curves (Fig. S12). The resulted ECSAs were 4.7, 1.4 and 0.8 mF∙cm− 2 for Cu HF, Cu foam and Cu foil, respectively. The ECSA ratio of Cu foam to Cu foil is 1.8, highly similar to their formate yield ratio (1.9) at − 1.1 V. Note that the ECSA of Cu HF is 3.4 and 5.9 times those of Cu foam and Cu foil, respectively, far lower than their formate yield disparities (16 and 30 times) at − 1.1 V, implying that the high ECSA only plays partial roles in efficiently producing formate over Cu HF electrode.
Fig. 5 show the schematic illustrations and the corresponding performances of Cu HF electrode by gas-diffusion mode and non-gasdiffusion mode, respectively. Within the whole potential range (− 0.4 to − 1.1 V), the generation of CO was well suppressed in gas-diffusion mode, resulting in CO FEs always less than 1% and formate FEs in 77–86% (Fig. 5B), implying the exclusive formation of formate during CO2ERR, especially 86% formate FE at − 0.9 V. The negative-shift potential from − 0.4 to − 1.1 V resulted in quick increases in current density from 6.5 to 210 mA∙cm− 2, and the almost constant current densities during the time span of 60 min at each given potential indicate the stable CO2 reduction. (Fig. S11). In contrast, the HER is much preferred in nongas-diffusion mode with H2 FEs higher than 50% at all given potentials and the CO FEs also increased to about 2%, which results in the formate FEs being only 40%–50% (Fig. 5C). The yield of formate at − 1.1 V was 1077 μmol h− 1 cm− 2, which was only 40% of the formate yield in gas-

diffusion mode at this potential. These results demonstrate that Cu HF using non-gas-diffusion mode delivers rather low electrocatalytic performances, which highlights the gas-diffusion effect in CO2ERR. That is the mass transport in gas-diffusion mode is greatly improved due to the reduced diffusion distance of CO2 in aqueous solution, resulting in efficient CO2 reduction to formate.

sections.heading: 3.3. Theoretical calculations
sections.text:
Cu HF distinguishes itself from the counterparts Cu foam and Cu foil in its unique hierarchical pore structures, which highly suit gas-diffusion mode and enable efficient CO2 electroreduction. During the forced penetration through the porous wall of Cu HF, the cone-shaped
structures (Fig. S13) on the surface induce to form a high local electric field, and CO2 molecules were frequently impacted with the metal substrate under such high electric field at first, which results in significant changes in bond angle and bond energy, as evidenced by molecular dynamics simulations (see SI and Fig. S14 for details). The bent O–C–O configuration is considered to be pre-activation of CO2 double bond, beneficial for further splitting carbon-oxygen bond [30,31]. Fig. 6 shows the variation of the most probable bond angle of CO2 with respect to the electric field intensity and pressure inside Cu HF micro-environment. High inner pressure (3.0 atm) and electric field intensity (108 V∙m− 1) enable a bond angle of 173.1◦ in bent CO2 molecules, accompanying an energy gain of 0.11 eV (Fig. S15). Subsequently, the stepwise proton-electron transfers of the bent CO2 molecules occurred at the
C. Zhu et al.
Journal of Power Sources 495 (2021) 229814
abundant gas-liquid-solid three-phase interfaces of Cu HF wall due to its appropriate hydrophilia (Fig. S16) [32].
To further explore the mechanism of selective formation of formate on Cu HF electrode, we conducted DFT calculations to investigate the pivotal intermediate energetics involved in CO2ERR (Fig. S17). Two pathways to CO or HCOOH on three metallic surfaces Cu (111), Cu (200) and Cu (220), respectively, are presented in Fig. 7. Although the reaction energy for the intermediate OCHO* via the first protonelectron transfer on Cu (111) is slightly high, the formation of HCOOH is preferred via the second proton-electron transfer on Cu (111) compared to Cu (200) and Cu (220) surfaces. Moreover, the energy barrier for forming COOH* on all Cu surfaces are much larger than those of the HCOOH pathway, resulting in CO only as a minor product
from CO2ERR. Note that the bent CO2 benefits to form OCHO* by virtue of lifting initial energy level, which further facilitates the HCOOH production. In addition, the energy barrier for forming H* is about 0.12 eV on Cu (220), much lower than those on Cu (111) and Cu (200) surfaces (Fig. 7), which is responsible for high H2 FE on Cu foil electrode from HER.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we report a distinct gas-diffusion configuration Cu HF electrode for highly efficient and stable electroreduction of CO2 to formate. The yield of formate reached 2677 μmol∙h− 1∙cm− 2 with a current density of 210 mA∙cm− 2 and a FE of 80%. The prominent electrocatalytic performance of the electrode is attributed to the unique pore structures providing abundant active sites and favorable mass transport as well as inducing the pre-activation of CO2, which synergistically facilitates the formate formation. This work provides an alternative for CO2 electroreduction, that is metallic hollow fibers are used to act as a more efficient gas-diffusion electrodes.
